prompt: In a chart of five overlapping lines, which part costs the reader most?

choices.why: Right. At each one the reader has to guess which line is which.
Nothing crosses it, so it is the easy one.
The months are shared and read once.
A title costs a second; crossings cost every reading.

prompt: Why are Centre-West and North hard to read on the five-line chart?

choices.text: They are squashed into the bottom tenth by the scale Southeast needs
choices.why: Right. Their shape is a few pixels tall.
Colour is not what hides their shape.

choices.text: They have fewer months of data
choices.why: All five have 24 months.
Order of drawing does not change their height.

prompt: What changes from panel to panel in a set of small multiples?

choices.why: Every panel uses the same chart type.
Keeping those the same is what makes the panels comparable.
Right. The frame repeats; the data changes.

choices.text: The size of each panel by importance
choices.why: Panels stay the same size, or the larger one looks more important.

prompt: Why draw the other regions in grey behind each panel's own line?

choices.text: To fill empty space in the panel
choices.why: Decoration is not the reason.

choices.text: So each line is seen in context
choices.why: Right. Northeast's panel shows it passing South.

choices.text: Because grey prints more cheaply than colour
choices.why: Cost has nothing to do with it.
The axis stays; the grey lines add comparison.

prompt: Twenty panels in one long row no longer fit on the screen. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Make each panel a different size
choices.why: Unequal sizes suggest unequal importance.

choices.text: Merge them back into one chart
choices.why: Twenty lines on one chart is the spaghetti again.
Right. About six to a row, then wrap.

choices.text: Drop the panels with the smallest values
choices.why: Dropping data hides it rather than laying it out.

prompt: With free scales, what did the small multiples lose?

choices.why: Shapes became easier to see, not harder.
The horizontal axis was unchanged.
The order was the same in both versions.
Right. North looked as big as Southeast.

prompt: The reader's question is "which region is biggest, and by how much?" Which scales should the panels use?

choices.why: Free scales make every region look the same size.
Right. Heights then compare across panels.
Without a scale the reader cannot say by how much.

choices.text: Free scales with the panels sorted by size
choices.why: Sorting helps the order, but free scales still hide the amounts.

prompt: A dashboard shows twelve stores as small multiples with free scales and no axis labels. A manager says store 7 sells as much as store 1. What is the likeliest explanation?

choices.text: The two stores really are the same size
choices.why: Possible, but nothing on this chart could show it.

choices.text: Every line fills its own panel, so heights mean nothing between panels
choices.why: Right. Unlabelled free scales are dual axes, repeated.

choices.text: The panels are in the wrong order
choices.why: Order does not change what each height means.
Twelve fits in a grid; the scales are the problem.

prompt: When free scales are used, what must the chart do?

choices.text: Draw the grey context lines in every panel
choices.why: With free scales those lines run off the edges.
Size does not tell the reader the scales differ.

choices.text: Say so in words and print each panel's axis values
choices.why: Right. Otherwise readers compare heights that cannot be compared.

choices.text: Use a different colour per panel
choices.why: Colour does not explain the scales.

prompt: Twelve monthly maps are drawn as small multiples. In what order do they go?

choices.why: Sorting months by value breaks the year.
April before August before December is no order at all.

choices.text: In the order of the file
choices.why: Usually the same as January to December, but that would be luck.
Right. Steps in time keep their order.

prompt: The regional panels are sorted by growth since January 2024. Which comes first?

choices.why: Southeast is first by size, but grew the least, to 159.
Northeast is second, at 260.
Right, with an index of 325.
South grew to 190, fourth of five.

prompt: When is alphabetical order acceptable for panels?

choices.why: Categories are usually better sorted by something meaningful.
Months keep their own order.
Scales and order are separate decisions.

choices.text: When there are many and readers look one up by name
choices.why: Right, and grouping by region first keeps neighbours together.

prompt: With free scales, North's panel ran from 423 to 1,517. How wide was that range, in orders?
In matplotlib, what does sharey=True do in subplots?

choices.why: Colours are set separately.

choices.text: Draws all the series in one panel
choices.why: That would undo the small multiples.

choices.text: Makes every panel use one vertical scale
choices.why: Right. Every panel then reported 57 to 8,590.
Each panel keeps its own title.

prompt: In a spreadsheet, you copy one formatted chart five times and change each copy's data. The axes were left on automatic. What have you built?

choices.text: Small multiples on one shared scale
choices.why: Each copy picks its own range on automatic.
Right. Fix the minimum and maximum before copying.
There is one axis per chart, but five charts.

choices.text: A chart with a truncated baseline
choices.why: Line charts may start above zero; the issue is that the five differ.

prompt: These small multiples share one scale, with the panels sorted largest first. Find each of these.

labels.text: the last month of the largest region
the panel of the smallest region

hint: The largest region's panel comes first.

prompt: Match each question to the scales it needs.

pairs.left: do they share a seasonal pattern?
do they differ by a hundredfold?

prompt: A set of small charts drawn the same way, each showing a different slice of the data, is called small ___.
Put the steps of building small multiples in a spreadsheet in order.
items: Fix its vertical axis minimum and maximum by hand
Change only the data range of each copy
trap: Fixing the axis after copying means fixing it five times, and missing one.

prompt: Who gave small multiples their name?

choices.why: Tukey gave us the boxplot, lesson 9.
Bertin named the visual variables, lesson 1.
Right, in The Visual Display of Quantitative Information.
Cleveland ranked the channels and proposed banking to 45 degrees.
